nature-econ-279.title: Hypothesis tests: could chance alone explain the data?
nature-econ-279.text: In 1710 John Arbuthnot asked whether male and female births in London were equally likely. His answer was the first statistical hypothesis test. Such a test uses sample data to decide whether a claim about a population, such as a drug lowering blood pressure, holds up. The population is the whole group of interest; the sample is the part actually measured. The test builds a model of what the data would look like if chance alone produced the results. That chance-only model is the {{ref:nature-econ-280}}. The test then asks how likely the actual data are under it. If the data are very unlikely, it is rejected. If not, the only conclusion is that the evidence against it is insufficient. A court trial works the same way: the default claim, like the defendant, is presumed true until evidence shows otherwise. Because a sample cannot settle the truth for certain, a test's conclusion can be wrong. Modern significance testing comes mainly from Karl Pearson, William Sealy Gosset and Ronald Fisher, while Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson developed hypothesis testing.

nature-econ-216.title: Correlation does not imply causation
nature-econ-216.text: Two things can rise and fall together without either causing the other. A correlation is simply that pattern of two variables moving together, and on its own it does not show that one causes the other. Treating a correlation as proof of cause is a logical fallacy known in Latin as cum hoc ergo propter hoc, 'with this, therefore because of this'. A correlation can mislead in two main ways. A hidden third factor can cause both variables, making them move together. Two unrelated variables can also correlate by pure chance, and the more things are examined, the more such accidental links turn up. Showing a cause usually takes four things: a correlation, the cause coming first, a plausible mechanism, and ruling out common or alternative causes. Dismissing correlation entirely is the opposite mistake, since much scientific evidence rests on variables observed together. Assumptions are always needed to draw causal conclusions, and modern {{ref:nature-econ-212}} focuses on testing how strong those assumptions are. In environmental medicine, many links could long be described only as correlations, because studies that show causation are hard or impossible to run. In economics, the 'credibility revolution' used better methods to tell correlation from causation.

nature-econ-212.title: Causal inference: finding what really causes what
nature-econ-212.text: Did the program cause the improvement, or would it have happened anyway? Causal inference is the process of working out the real, separate effect of one thing that is part of a larger system. Unlike finding an association, it asks how an outcome responds when one of its causes is changed. One description has three steps. Establish that cause and effect vary together, show that the cause comes first, and rule out other plausible causes. Because correlation does not imply causation ({{ref:nature-econ-216}}), the work is as much about plausible mechanisms as about patterns in data. It is especially hard where experiments are difficult or impossible, which is common in most sciences. Economics is a prime case. Real economies are complex, and many large events cannot be recreated in controlled experiments. Economists therefore increasingly look for events that mimic an experiment ({{ref:nature-econ-243}}), and randomized field experiments help deal with hidden distorting factors. Many social scientists adopted Donald Rubin's potential outcomes framework as a standard for inferring causality. Critics say economists and social scientists still often pass off descriptive studies as causal ones.

nature-econ-242.title: The Monte Carlo method: solving problems with dice
nature-econ-242.text: Stanisław Ulam, the method's main developer, was inspired by his uncle's gambling, and it is named after the Monte Carlo Casino. The Monte Carlo method is a family of computer techniques that get numerical answers by repeated random sampling. The idea is to use randomness to solve problems that are not random in themselves. The simplest version estimates an average, an {{ref:nature-econ-756}}, by running many simulations and averaging the results. Rather than one 'what if' scenario built on best-guess values, it samples each uncertain variable from a probability distribution. The result is hundreds or thousands of possible outcomes. Its main uses are optimization, numerical integration and drawing samples, especially when inputs are very uncertain. It can be costly to compute, but the runs are independent, so they can be spread across many processors. In {{ref:nature-val-001}} it supports formal risk analysis of uncertain costs and benefits. The IPCC relies on it to analyze the probability distributions of {{ref:nature-eco-004}}.

nature-econ-273.title: Sensitivity analysis: which assumptions drive the answer?
nature-econ-273.text: Models in fields like climate science or economics can be so complex that how their inputs drive their outputs is poorly understood. Sensitivity analysis studies how the uncertainty in a model's output can be traced back to, and shared among, the uncertain inputs that feed it ({{ref:nature-econ-152}}). Inputs can be uncertain because of measurement errors, missing information, poor understanding of mechanisms, or the choice of underlying hypothesis ({{ref:nature-econ-772}}). The analysis is almost always done by running the model many times with sampled inputs, which can be computationally expensive. In {{ref:nature-val-001}} it shows how results respond when parameters change. The European Commission, the US Office of Management and Budget, the IPCC and the US EPA all include it in their guidelines. Leamer's global sensitivity analysis sets a demanding standard. A conclusion counts as sturdy only if a credibly wide range of assumptions still gives a usefully narrow range of inferences.

nature-econ-218.title: Designing experiments that can reveal causes
nature-econ-218.text: Ronald Fisher worked out much of modern experimental method for agriculture. His books The Arrangement of Field Experiments (1926) and The Design of Experiments (1935) set out how to plan a test. Design of experiments means planning procedures that test how changing one part of a system leads to changes in other parts ({{ref:nature-econ-212}}). It decides which parts to change and which to hold fixed, based on hypotheses about what drives variation. The changed inputs are independent variables; the outcomes they should change are dependent variables. Charles S. Peirce had already stressed randomization-based inference in publications of 1877–1878 and 1883. Only when participants are randomly chosen and randomly assigned can differences in outcomes be confidently put down to the different conditions. The main concerns are validity, reliability and replicability, along with enough statistical power to detect an effect. Laws and ethics rule out some well-designed experiments on people, through review boards, informed consent and confidentiality. Valuing nature uses the craft too. Choice experiments that value environmental goods depend on a design that controls which hypothetical scenarios respondents see.

nature-econ-211.title: Bayesian inference: updating beliefs as evidence arrives
nature-econ-211.text: Thomas Bayes (1701–1761) gave the method his name, but Pierre-Simon Laplace introduced what is now called Bayes' theorem. Bayesian inference uses that theorem to work out how likely a hypothesis is from earlier evidence, and to update the probability as new information arrives. It starts from a prior distribution, the belief about a quantity before any data are seen, and turns it into posterior probabilities. Updating suits data that arrive in sequence: the posterior from one stage becomes the prior for the next. Early versions were called inverse probability, because they reason backward from effects to causes. Abraham Wald showed that every unique Bayesian procedure is admissible, which made Bayesian methods central even to rival approaches to estimation and {{ref:nature-econ-279}}. Complex models often cannot be solved by formula, so Bayesian analysis leans on {{ref:nature-econ-242}} simulation such as Gibbs sampling. The approach is used in science, engineering, medicine, sport, psychology and law.

nature-econ-239.title: Maximum likelihood: the settings that best explain the data
nature-econ-239.text: Given some data and an assumed shape for the process behind them, which settings make the observed data most probable? Maximum likelihood estimation answers that. It estimates the parameters of an assumed probability distribution by choosing the values under which the observed data are most likely, an exercise in {{ref:nature-econ-461}}. Ronald Fisher created the modern method between 1912 and 1922, building on Gauss, Laplace and others. Its logic is intuitive and flexible, and it has become a dominant way of doing statistical inference. With enough data it is consistent, homing in on the true value with arbitrary precision. Except in special cases its equations must be solved step by step from an initial guess. It matches the most probable Bayesian estimate when the prior is uniform ({{ref:nature-econ-211}}). One weakness is that its predictions ignore the uncertainty in the estimated parameters. Probit and logit models, including those used for {{ref:nature-val-100}}, are typically estimated this way.

nature-econ-246.title: Panel data: following the same subjects over time
nature-econ-246.text: A panel of 130 countries followed from 1975 to 2010 found obesity rising with income in poor settings and falling in rich ones. That study used panel data: data that follow the same subjects, such as people, firms or countries, with repeated measurements over time. Time series (one subject over time) and cross-sectional data (many subjects at one time) are one-dimensional special cases. In a balanced panel every subject is observed in every period; in an unbalanced panel some are missing. Panels help with a stubborn problem. Unchanging traits, such as a country's geography or climate, can bias a standard {{ref:nature-econ-257}} if they are correlated with the explanatory variables. The methods in {{ref:nature-econ-227}} and {{ref:nature-econ-228}} can control for such traits. Random effects is more efficient when the traits are uncorrelated with the explanatory variables. Using a past outcome as an explanatory variable creates dynamic panel data, which needs special methods such as the Arellano–Bond estimator.

nature-econ-280.title: The null hypothesis: assuming no effect until proven otherwise
nature-econ-280.text: For a heart-attack drug, a possible null hypothesis is that the drug has no effect on the risk of a heart attack. The null hypothesis is the default claim that a measured quantity, usually a difference or effect, is zero. A test weighs it against its negation, the alternative hypothesis ({{ref:nature-econ-279}}). The null is what the evidence must overturn. Paul Meehl raised a sharp objection. When the null is simply 'no effect', he argued, a more precise experiment is a less severe test of the theory behind it.

nature-econ-281.title: P-values: measuring how surprising a result is
nature-econ-281.text: How surprising is a result, if nothing is really going on? A p-value puts a number on that. It is the probability of getting a test result at least as extreme as the one observed if the null hypothesis were true ({{ref:nature-econ-280}}). If the p-value is at or below the test's significance level, written alpha, the null is rejected. The threshold is usually set so that results this extreme would occur less than 5% or 1% of the time under the null. Two cautions matter. A rejection does not mean the chance that the null is true is below alpha. And statistical significance does not imply practical significance: a detectable effect is not necessarily an important one.

nature-econ-282.title: Type I and type II errors: two ways a test can fail
nature-econ-282.text: Every test can go wrong in two ways. A type I error rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true, a false positive. A type II error keeps a null hypothesis when the alternative is true, a false negative ({{ref:nature-econ-280}}). The probability of a type I error equals the test's significance level. A typical randomized trial accepts a 0.05, or 1 in 20, chance of wrongly finding two equally effective treatments different. One minus the probability of a type II error is called the test's power, its ability to catch a real effect. Large samples are recommended to reduce type II errors.

nature-econ-219.title: Random assignment: letting chance pick the groups
nature-econ-219.text: Chance is the experimenter's most useful ally. Random assignment puts people or units into an experiment's groups by chance, so each has the same chance of ending up in any group ({{ref:nature-econ-218}}). It is what separates a true experiment from an observational study or {{ref:nature-econ-214}}. It does not remove hidden distorting factors ({{ref:nature-econ-213}}), but it tends to balance known and unknown ones between groups on average. Without it, outcome differences between groups are likely due to some third variable. Comparing treatments against a control or standard treatment as a baseline is usually more valuable than isolated measurements.

nature-econ-254.title: Randomized controlled trials: the gold-standard experiment
nature-econ-254.text: In a book published in 1648, Jan Baptist van Helmont proposed comparing two fever treatments by assigning patients at random. It was the first proposal for a randomized controlled trial (RCT). An RCT tests an intervention by assigning participants to comparison groups at random ({{ref:nature-econ-219}}), which limits bias. At least one group gets the intervention, while others get an alternative, a placebo or standard care. Proper randomization removes bias in who gets treated, specifically {{ref:nature-econ-270}} and confounding. That is why RCTs are seen as the most reliable evidence in healthcare. They reduce spurious causality and bias, and their results can be pooled in a {{ref:nature-nbs-094}}. They have weaknesses too. If a treatment's effect is small, too few participants may make it impossible to reject the null hypothesis. They can be costly: 28 Phase III trials funded by one US institute before 2000 cost US$335 million in total, a mean of US$12 million each. And withholding an obviously beneficial treatment from a control group can make an RCT unethical.

nature-econ-243.title: Natural experiments: when the world assigns the treatment
nature-econ-243.text: In 1854 cholera broke out around Broad Street in London. John Snow compared water drawn above and below London's sewage outfalls, in one of the best-known early natural experiments. In such a study, nature or other forces outside the researchers' control decide who is exposed to a condition and who is not ({{ref:nature-econ-212}}). The exposure may resemble random assignment, but these remain observational studies, not controlled ones. They are most reliable when a clear exposure hits a well-defined group while a comparable group stays unexposed. They are used where controlled experiments would be extremely difficult or unethical, as often in epidemiology and economics. Angrist used the Vietnam War draft lottery in this way ({{ref:nature-econ-234}}) and found veterans earned about 15 percent less than non-veterans. Nature runs its own trials too. When air pollution fell in the twentieth century, dark forms of the peppered moth quickly became scarce again. The drawback is that, without control over variables, investigators may be unable to draw firm conclusions.

nature-econ-230.title: Counterfactuals: comparing reality with what might have been
nature-econ-230.text: What would have happened without the program? Counterfactual analysis compares what actually happened with that unseen alternative. The counterfactual is the outcome beneficiaries would have had without the intervention, and impact is the gap between it and what was observed ({{ref:nature-econ-212}}). The key difficulty is that the counterfactual can never be observed directly. It must be approximated with a comparison group, set up in advance (prospective) or found afterward (retrospective). In {{ref:nature-econ-221}}, for example, the control group stands in for the counterfactual.

nature-econ-267.title: The Rubin causal model: two possible lives for every unit
nature-econ-267.text: A person would have one income at age 40 if they went to college and another if they did not. The causal effect of college compares the two. That is the core of the Rubin causal model. A treatment's effect is the difference between the outcomes a unit would have with and without it, its potential outcomes ({{ref:nature-econ-230}}). Jerzy Neyman first proposed potential outcomes in his 1923 master's thesis. Donald Rubin extended the idea from experiments to observational studies. Randomized experiments can estimate causal effects for a population, because random assignment makes groups equivalent on average ({{ref:nature-econ-219}}). The average treatment effect is the mean of all the individual effects. How units are assigned matters: a 'perfect doctor' who gives each patient whatever suits them best distorts the comparison of averages. A causal effect is defined only if both outcomes could happen. Height cannot be manipulated, so its causal effect on weight makes no sense in this framework.

nature-econ-229.title: Impact evaluation: did the program cause the change?
nature-econ-229.text: Hitting a target is not the same as causing it. Impact evaluation assesses how far a project, program or policy actually caused the outcomes seen, intended or not. Unlike monitoring whether targets were met, it asks how outcomes would have changed had the intervention not happened ({{ref:nature-econ-230}}). It answers the questions of evidence-based policy: what works, what doesn't, where, why and for how much. Randomized field experiments are the strongest designs when feasible. Otherwise evaluators turn to methods such as matching, differencing and {{ref:nature-econ-234}}. Whatever design is chosen, every one can yield biased estimates. The best-known early large-scale experimental evaluation was of Mexico's Progresa, a program of cash payments tied to conditions. Theory-based evaluation goes further, mapping the causal chain from inputs to outcomes rather than only reporting average differences between groups.

nature-econ-249.title: Program evaluation: does it work, and is it worth it?
nature-econ-249.text: Funders, voters and others often want to know whether the programs they support deliver the promised effect. Program evaluation is a systematic way of collecting and using information to judge whether projects, policies and programs work and whether they are good value for money ({{ref:nature-econ-229}}). An evaluation can examine needs, the logic behind a program, its implementation, its impact and its efficiency, at different stages of its life. It overlaps with {{ref:nature-val-001}}, but social outcomes can be harder to assess than market outcomes and need different skills. The hardest part is often showing that the program itself, rather than outside events, caused the observed changes. Practical gaps add to the difficulty. Many projects include no budget for evaluation, and one started late may have no baseline data from before the program began. Environmental credits face a similar check. The test of {{ref:nature-mkt-144}} may be applied after the fact, as program evaluation often does, or beforehand as a screen for issuing credits.

nature-econ-268.title: The fundamental problem of causal inference
nature-econ-268.text: A patient cannot both take a pill and not take it over the same period. That simple fact is the fundamental problem of causal inference. No one can observe both potential outcomes for the same unit, so individual causal effects cannot be seen directly ({{ref:nature-econ-267}}). This does not make causal inference impossible. Certain techniques and assumptions get around it, and assumptions are needed to estimate the missing counterfactual outcomes.

nature-econ-283.title: The case against significance testing
nature-econ-283.text: Few statistical tools are as widely used, or as widely criticized, as null hypothesis significance testing ({{ref:nature-econ-279}}). Critics argue it is misunderstood, overused and misused, and should not be the only tool of analysis. Modern practice is a hybrid of Fisher's approach and Neyman and Pearson's, which critics say causes confusion. Rigidly requiring significance for publication produces {{ref:nature-econ-241}}. Many critics prefer estimation statistics, reporting an estimated value with an interval rather than an accept-or-reject verdict. The two sides agree on how the method works but disagree on what to do: some critics would ban it completely, while supporters prefer a less absolute change.

nature-econ-214.title: Quasi-experiments: testing causes without a lab
nature-econ-214.text: Some experiments cannot be run. They may cost too much, involve systems as large as whole economies, or endanger the people involved. A quasi-experiment tests a cause-and-effect claim without a true controlled experiment ({{ref:nature-econ-212}}). Treatments are given as if at random, for example in elections won by very slim margins. Without controlled experiments, econometricians often look for natural experiments ({{ref:nature-econ-243}}) or apply quasi-experimental methods.

nature-econ-275.title: One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis: turning one knob
nature-econ-275.text: The simplest way to probe a model is to turn one knob at a time. One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis changes a single input while holding the others at baseline values, and watches how the output responds ({{ref:nature-econ-273}}). The input then returns to its baseline, and the step is repeated for each other input. Like local derivative-based methods, it examines small changes one variable at a time. It does not explore the full range of inputs.

nature-econ-277.title: Sensitivity auditing: questioning a model's framing
nature-econ-277.text: A model's numbers can be checked, and so can the question it was built to answer. Sensitivity auditing extends {{ref:nature-econ-273}} to the framing, institutional context and motives behind a model whose results feed policy decisions. Framing can carry unstated assumptions. Some are political, such as which group needs protecting. Others are technical, such as which variable is treated as constant.

nature-econ-276.title: Variance-based sensitivity analysis: sharing out the uncertainty
nature-econ-276.text: Which uncertain input matters most? Variance-based sensitivity analysis treats inputs and outputs as random variables. It splits the output's variance, its spread, into shares caused by each input and each combination of inputs ({{ref:nature-econ-273}}). The shares are calculated as Sobol indices, the proportion of output variance explained by an input or group of inputs. The first-order index measures one input's contribution alone, averaged over variations in the others.

nature-econ-220.title: P-hacking: reanalyzing until the answer looks right
nature-econ-220.text: A result that clears the bar of significance may have been nudged over it. P-hacking is trying many analyses, often unconsciously, until one gives the result the researcher wanted ({{ref:nature-econ-281}}). It usually means adjusting the analysis until a result falls below the p<.05 level of statistical significance. Such false positives often come from pressure to publish or from the author's own confirmation bias. Preregistration, sending the analysis plan to a journal before collecting data, can prevent it. Double-blind designs, where researchers do not know who is in which group, stop them influencing participants' responses.

nature-econ-256.title: Blinding: keeping knowledge from skewing a trial
nature-econ-256.text: What people in a trial know can skew what it finds. Blinding means keeping participants, caregivers or outcome assessors from knowing which intervention each person received ({{ref:nature-econ-254}}). A placebo, a dummy treatment, in the control group lets participants stay unaware of which treatment they got. Blinding is sometimes impossible, as when a treatment such as physical therapy needs the patient's active participation.

nature-econ-255.title: Randomized trials come to economics
nature-econ-255.text: In 1994 Paul Glewwe, Michael Kremer and Sylvie Moulin began one of the earliest economic randomized trials, a long-run school intervention in Kenya. Randomized controlled trials have since become a standard way to identify causal effects in economics, especially in development economics ({{ref:nature-econ-254}}). They helped bolster the credibility revolution in empirical microeconomics. Since 2013 the American Economic Association registry has tracked over 7,400 field experiments across 100 countries. Their spread has not settled the argument, however. Economists and other social scientists remain divided over how far RCTs should be used in their fields.

nature-econ-217.title: Reverse causation: mistaking the effect for the cause
nature-econ-217.text: Windmills turn faster when there is more wind, but that does not mean windmills make wind. Reverse causation is the mistake of reading cause and effect the wrong way round, treating the effect as the cause ({{ref:nature-econ-216}}). Real cases are subtler. Low cholesterol goes with higher death rates partly because diseases such as cancer lower cholesterol and also raise mortality. Two things can also each partly cause the other, such as poverty and lack of education. Where controlled experiments cannot settle the direction of causation, as often in the social sciences, the confusion can fuel long scientific arguments.

nature-econ-213.title: Confounding variables: the hidden third factor
nature-econ-213.text: A confounder hides in plain sight. A confounding variable strongly affects a study's results but is not the thing whose effect the study is trying to measure ({{ref:nature-econ-212}}). The classic case is a third factor that causes both A and B, making A and B move together. Confounders make results unstable: one can make a factor look important in one version of a model and unimportant in another. In impact evaluation, confounding often comes from socioeconomic factors linked both to who receives a program and to the outcome. The standard defense is chance. Assigning units to treatments at random tends to balance known and unknown confounders between groups on average ({{ref:nature-econ-219}}).

nature-econ-270.title: Selection bias: when the sample tells the wrong story
nature-econ-270.text: Volunteers may differ from the people a study means to describe; studies find they tend to come from higher social standing. That is one face of selection bias. It arises when the people, groups or data chosen for analysis are picked in a skewed way. The link between exposure and outcome in the sample then differs from the link among everyone eligible. It typically occurs when researchers filter or adjust on a factor that both the exposure and the outcome influence, creating a false association ({{ref:nature-econ-213}}). The family includes loss to follow-up, volunteer bias, healthy-worker bias and nonresponse bias. In general it cannot be fixed by analyzing existing data alone, though the Heckman correction works in special cases. Ecology is affected too: researchers' choices of where to study may bias modern estimates of biodiversity.

nature-econ-272.title: Attrition bias: the problem of people who drop out
nature-econ-272.text: In a diet trial, dropping everyone who quits biases the results, because most quitters are those for whom the diet was not working. That is attrition bias, a form of {{ref:nature-econ-270}} caused by losing participants, such as dropouts and non-responders, during a study. It is closely related to survivorship bias, where only subjects that survived a process are analyzed.

nature-econ-271.title: Sampling bias: when some people are easier to count
nature-econ-271.text: A sample is meant to stand in for a whole population. Sampling bias is the systematic error that arises when it is not random, so some members of the population were less likely to be included than others. It is usually treated as a kind of {{ref:nature-econ-270}}, though some classify it separately. One view holds that sampling bias threatens how far results generalize, while selection bias mainly threatens comparisons within the sample. Examples include self-selection and the pre-screening of trial participants.

nature-econ-253.title: The back-door criterion: spotting confounders in a diagram
nature-econ-253.text: Judea Pearl turned the hunt for confounders into a drawing exercise. In a causal diagram, arrows run from causes to effects. The back-door criterion is Pearl's graphical test for spotting confounding variables in such a diagram ({{ref:nature-econ-213}}). To estimate a treatment's effect, the background variables chosen must block every back-door path in the graph. A path can be blocked by adding the confounder as a control in a {{ref:nature-econ-257}}, or by matching on it.

nature-econ-269.title: SUTVA: when one person's treatment affects another
nature-econ-269.text: If Mary's drug makes her cook with more salt, Joe's blood pressure depends on her treatment too. That breaks the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA), which requires that one unit's outcome is unaffected by which treatment other units receive ({{ref:nature-econ-267}}). Field experiments call it the non-interference assumption. Violations make causal inference harder, though dependence can be handled by considering more treatments.

nature-econ-251.title: Reliability and validity: can a measure be trusted?
nature-econ-251.text: A poorly chosen measure can undermine an impact assessment completely by producing misleading estimates ({{ref:nature-econ-249}}). Two qualities guard against that. Reliability is how far a measure gives the same result each time it measures the same thing. Validity is how far it measures what it is meant to measure. The more reliable a measure is, the greater its statistical power and the more credible its findings. A measure must also be sensitive enough to detect the changes a program might cause.

nature-econ-250.title: Program theory: the bet built into every program
nature-econ-250.text: Every program carries a built-in bet about how its actions will lead to the outcomes it wants. That bet is its program theory, or logic model ({{ref:nature-econ-249}}). Program staff often leave it unstated. An evaluator must then draw it out of them and judge whether it is plausible.

nature-econ-231.title: The randomistas debate over development
nature-econ-231.text: William Easterly called it 'The Civil War in Development economics'. The randomistas debate is the argument over whether randomized experiments should be the main way to evaluate development programs ({{ref:nature-econ-254}}). Supporters, called 'randomistas', say randomization is the only way to deal with selection bias from factors no one can observe. Critics say random assignment rarely suits development interventions and gives results for one context with little wider relevance. The two camps still openly disagree about how such programs should be evaluated.

nature-econ-232.title: Secular trends and maturation: change that would happen anyway
nature-econ-232.text: A fertility program may look effective simply because the community's birth rate was already falling. A health program for adults may look ineffective because health generally declines with age. Both traps are secular trends and maturation: changes that would happen anyway during a program and can bias estimates of its effect ({{ref:nature-econ-229}}). They include long-term trends, short-term events and people aging. The defense is to keep program and control groups in comparable circumstances.

openers.empirical-methods-and-econometrics: Economists cannot rerun history, so they must learn from data, and this chapter covers the methods for doing that well. A statistical hypothesis test starts from a default claim that an effect is zero, then asks how probable a result at least as extreme as the one observed would be if that claim were true. The deeper challenge is cause: two things moving together does not, on its own, show that one causes the other. Causal inference works to isolate the real, separate effect of one thing inside a larger system, with help from planned experiments, data that follow the same subjects over time, and estimation methods that pick the values making the observed data most probable. Repeated random sampling on computers, sensitivity analysis and Bayesian updating help show how much confidence the answers deserve.
